units.title: How to read the Bible
units.eq: How does God speak in Scripture?

lessons.title: God’s word in human words
lessons.idea: God is the author of Scripture and the human writers are true authors who used their own gifts, style and world. We take both seriously: God’s word in human words. Because of this the Bible is without error in what God wanted to teach for our salvation.
lessons.question: If God is the author, why do the books differ in style?
lessons.activity: “Two accounts, one event” (30 min). Read the feeding of the five thousand in Matthew 14, Mark 6 and John 6 side by side. Students list shared details and differences. Ask what each author emphasizes and why. Conclude: the differences show human authors, the agreement shows one story God wants told.
teach: God is the author of Scripture; inspired human authors wrote “all and only” what he wanted (CCC 105–107; Dei Verbum 11). 2 Timothy 3:16 says all Scripture is “God-breathed.”
The human authors are “true authors” using their faculties and context (CCC 106). To read well we must ask what they meant (CCC 109–110).
Because the Spirit is the author, Scripture teaches “firmly, faithfully and without error” the truth for our salvation (CCC 107). This does not make it a science textbook.
The Church warns against fundamentalism, which ignores literary forms, and against skepticism, which denies inspiration.
talk: If God is the author, why do the books sound different?
Which passage raises questions for you?
quiz: Who is the author of Scripture?|Only angels|God, through human authors|Only humans|The Church alone|1|CCC 105-106.
Inerrancy means Scripture teaches…|Without error what God wanted for our salvation|Everything about science|Only poetry|Nothing|0|CCC 107.
Biblical authors are…|Ghostwriters|Unknown|Secretaries only|True authors|3|Dei Verbum 11.
lessons.life: Read one chapter of a Gospel slowly this week and write one question.
lessons.saint: Jerome: patron of Scripture scholars.
misc: “God dictated every word like a secretary.”
“The Bible is just human opinion about God.”
lessons.mem: “All Scripture is inspired by God and profitable for teaching, for reproof, for correction, and for training in righteousness.” (2 Timothy 3:16)
lessons.hook: Show a letter from a parent written in a child’s own handwriting style. “Whose is it?” Both. The Bible is like that: God’s message through real authors.
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain in a few sentences how God and human authors both wrote Scripture.

lessons.title: Literary forms and the senses of Scripture
lessons.idea: To understand Scripture we must notice the literary form (history, poetry, law, prophecy, parable, letter, apocalypse) and read for the senses of Scripture: the literal sense, and the spiritual senses (allegorical, moral, anagogical).
lessons.question: What is the difference between literal and spiritual senses?
lessons.activity: “Form sort and the four senses” (30 min). Cards with Bible passages (Genesis 1, Leviticus 19, Psalm 23, Isaiah 53, Matthew 5, Romans 8, Revelation 21). Students sort by form. Then take Jonah’s three days: literal (what happens), allegorical (Christ’s tomb, Matthew 12:40), moral (obey God), anagogical (resurrection hope).
teach: Read with attention to literary genres and the author’s intention (CCC 109–110). Genesis 1 uses a literary structure to teach that God is the source and all is good.
The literal sense is what the words convey (CCC 116). The spiritual senses build on it: allegorical (how events point to Christ), moral (how to act) and anagogical (heavenly destiny) (CCC 115–117).
In Luke 24:25–27 Jesus explains how “all the Scriptures” point to him. The Old Testament is fulfilled in him (CCC 128–130).
Read all of Scripture in the light of Christ, the unity of the whole Bible and the Church’s living Tradition (CCC 112–114).
talk: How does knowing the genre change reading?
quiz: The literal sense is…|What the author intended to say|An allegory only|A scientific reading|A fantasy|0|CCC 116.
The senses of Scripture are literal and…|Scientific|Silly|Spiritual|Political|2|CCC 115.
Wisdom literature includes…|Genesis|Acts|Proverbs and Job|Exodus|2|CCC 120.
lessons.life: Identify the genre of tonight’s reading before you read it.
lessons.saint: Augustine: taught that Scripture must be read in light of charity.
misc: “Reading a text figuratively means it is not true.”
lessons.mem: “Beginning with Moses and all the prophets, he interpreted to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself.” (Luke 24:27)
lessons.hook: Ask: “Do you read a recipe the way you read a poem?” Read two lines of different kinds and ask how each should be taken.
lessons.assess: Give a passage and ask students to name its literary form and one spiritual sense.

lessons.title: Scripture, Tradition and the Magisterium
lessons.idea: Scripture, Tradition and the Magisterium work together. Scripture and Tradition flow from the same divine source; the Magisterium (the Pope and bishops) authentically interprets them. None stands alone.
lessons.question: Why do Catholics rely on Tradition as well as the Bible?
lessons.activity: “Three witnesses” (25 min). Students use Acts 2:42, 2 Thessalonians 2:15 and the Jerusalem Council (Acts 15) to show how apostles taught by word and writing, and decided disputes with authority. Draw a diagram with arrows among Scripture, Tradition, Magisterium. Explain it to a partner.
teach: Sacred Tradition and Sacred Scripture “flow out of the same divine wellspring” (CCC 80–82). Tradition is the living transmission of the Gospel, not just customs.
The Church wrote the New Testament and determined the canon under the Spirit’s guidance (CCC 120). The Magisterium is “not above the Word of God, but serves it” (CCC 86).
Paul told the Thessalonians to “hold to the traditions you were taught, whether by word of mouth or by letter” (2 Thessalonians 2:15). Acts 15 shows a council deciding authoritatively.
Contrast gently with the Protestant principle sola scriptura, which the Church does not accept, but avoid caricature.
talk: Why does the Church read Scripture with Tradition?
quiz: The deposit of faith is…|Scripture and Tradition|Only Tradition|Opinions|Only Scripture|0|CCC 84.
The Magisterium is…|A council only|A hymn|A book|The teaching office of the Church|3|CCC 85.
Tradition is…|A story|A custom|The Gospel handed on|A rule|2|CCC 78.
lessons.life: Learn who the successor of Peter and your bishop are.
lessons.saint: Irenaeus: apostolic Tradition.
misc: “Tradition means old customs that can change anytime.”
“The Church put the Bible above itself.”
lessons.mem: “They devoted themselves to the apostles’ teaching and fellowship, to the breaking of bread and the prayers.” (Acts 2:42)
lessons.hook: Show a three-legged stool, then remove a leg. “What happens?” Use it as a way to picture how the three support each other (while noting the analogy is limited).
lessons.assess: Ask students to define each of the three and explain how they fit together.

lessons.title: Creation: a gift
lessons.idea: Genesis 1–2 teach that God created everything freely and that all is good. Humans, made in his image, are the summit of creation and are called to care for the world. The Sabbath is the crown of creation.
lessons.question: What does Genesis 1 teach?
lessons.activity: “Genesis 1 theology chart” (30 min). Students read Genesis 1:1–2:4 and list the claims: one God, creation by word, order, goodness, humanity in God’s image, Sabbath. Compare with Babylonian creation myths (the gods fight and humans are slaves). What is different?
teach: Creation is a gift out of nothing, ordered and good (CCC 279–301). God needs nothing; creation is the first act of love.
Humans are created male and female in God’s image (Genesis 1:27; CCC 355–357). That gives every person equal dignity and the vocation to know and love God.
The Sabbath is the goal of creation; worship is built into the world (CCC 345–349). The second account (Genesis 2) shows the intimacy of God with Adam and Eve.
Caring for creation (stewardship) is a duty (CCC 2415–2418). Pope Francis’ Laudato Si’ develops this.
talk: What does Genesis 1 teach about God?
What does it teach about humans?
quiz: Creation ex nihilo means…|From a rock|Out of nothing|From a god|From chaos|1|CCC 296.
Humans are made…|Without a soul|In God’s image|From angels|By chance|1|CCC 355.
On the seventh day God…|Rested|Left|Destroyed|Created more|0|Genesis 2:2.
lessons.life: Keep a Sabbath rest from screens for a few hours.
lessons.saint: Francis: Canticle.
misc: “Genesis 1 and 2 contradict each other, so the Bible is unreliable.”
“Humans may use creation however they want.”
lessons.mem: “So God created man in his own image, in the image of God he created him; male and female he created them.” (Genesis 1:27)
lessons.hook: Play two clips: a news story about a storm and a video of a beautiful sunrise. “Both are in the same world. How can the world be good and still have trouble?” The next lessons answer.
lessons.assess: Ask students to list three truths taught by Genesis 1.

lessons.title: The fall
lessons.idea: Genesis 3 is the story of the fall: Adam and Eve, tempted by the serpent, chose their own way over God’s. The result was broken trust, shame, suffering and death. The Church calls the root of this original sin.
lessons.question: How does sin spread?
lessons.activity: “What, how, why” (25 min). In small groups, answer three questions from Genesis 3: What did they do? (disobeyed God’s command) How did it happen? (doubt: “Did God really say?”, pride) Why does it matter? (broken relationships with God, each other, creation). Then read Genesis 3:15 and Romans 5:18–19.
teach: Original sin is the first sin, a loss of original holiness, and its inheritance is a human nature wounded (CCC 396–405). It is transmitted by propagation, not imitation (CCC 404).
The temptation begins with doubt about God’s goodness (CCC 397). The result: shame, blame, pain, death and alienation (CCC 399–400).
Jesus is the new Adam who undoes the disobedience by his obedience (Romans 5:18–19; CCC 411). Baptism removes original sin (CCC 405).
The story is a true account in figurative language of a primeval event (CCC 390). Avoid fixating on the apple.
quiz: Original sin is…|A recent sin|A story|A state of fallen nature|A rule|2|CCC 404.
Concupiscence is…|Joy|Habit of prayer|Courage|Inclination to sin|3|CCC 405.
The first promise of a Redeemer is in…|Exodus 3|Psalm 23|Isaiah 7|Genesis 3:15|3|CCC 410.
lessons.life: Make an act of trust each time you notice temptation.
lessons.saint: Mary: new Eve.
misc: “Original sin means babies are guilty of a personal sin.”
lessons.mem: “As by one man’s disobedience many were made sinners, so by one man’s obedience many will be made righteous.” (Romans 5:19)
lessons.hook: Show a broken mirror. “What breaks when we disobey?” Take answers and note that trust is the first thing to go.
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain what happened in the fall and what remedy God gave.

lessons.title: Cain and Abel; Noah; Babel
lessons.idea: In Genesis 4–11 sin spreads: Cain kills Abel, the world fills with violence and God sends the flood, and humans try to “make a name” at Babel. Yet God keeps saving: he protects Cain, rescues Noah’s family and makes a covenant, and finally calls Abram.
lessons.question: What do these stories show?
lessons.activity: “Timeline of Genesis 1–11” (25 min). Students draw a timeline with events and for each add: the sin, God’s response and the promise. Highlight the covenant sign: the rainbow (Genesis 9:12–17). End by asking, “Why does God choose Abram next?”
teach: Cain’s murder shows sin turning into hatred of a brother (CCC 2259). God asks, “Where is your brother?” God is a protector of life even for the guilty.
The flood story shows God’s judgment and mercy: Noah’s ark prefigures the Church and Baptism (CCC 56–58, 845, 1219; 1 Peter 3:20–21). The covenant with Noah includes all creation.
Babel shows human pride dividing nations; Pentecost reverses it (CCC 56, 674). God’s response is to start a new work with Abram.
The “remnant” theme runs through the Bible: God preserves a faithful few to renew the many.
quiz: God’s covenant with Noah included…|Only kings|Only Israel|All creation|Only priests|2|Genesis 9:9-10.
Babel shows…|Joy|Peace|Pride|Obedience|2|Genesis 11.
The flood story points to…|Passover|Pentecost|Baptism|Christmas|2|1 Peter 3:20-21.
lessons.life: Examine pride in your own heart.
lessons.saint: Noah: a righteous man who trusted God and built the ark.
lessons.mem: “I establish my covenant with you, that never again shall all flesh be cut off by the waters of the flood.” (Genesis 9:11)
lessons.hook: Draw a staircase going down with the labels Eden, Cain, Flood, Babel. Ask what pattern appears. Then add a second staircase going up with God’s mercy each time.
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain how each story shows both sin and God’s mercy.

units.title: The patriarchs
units.eq: How does God choose a people?

lessons.title: Abraham: father of faith
lessons.idea: God called Abram to leave home and promised him descendants, land and a blessing for all nations. Abraham believed, and it was counted to him as righteousness. He is the father of all who believe.
lessons.question: Why is Abraham our father in faith?
lessons.activity: “Abraham’s journey map” (30 min). Trace the route from Ur to Haran to Canaan to Egypt and back, marking altars, the covenant of Genesis 15 (stars, fire pot) and 17 (circumcision, name change). Write one sentence at each stop on what Abraham trusted.
teach: Abraham is “our father in faith” (CCC 59, 145–147; Romans 4). God’s call began a new people through whom the world would be blessed (Genesis 12:3).
In Genesis 15 God swears a covenant with fire passing between the animals: God takes the risk. Abraham “believed the Lord, and he counted it to him as righteousness” (Genesis 15:6; Romans 4:3).
Genesis 17 changes his name to Abraham, “father of a multitude.” Circumcision is the sign.
Abraham is honored by Jews, Christians and Muslims. Vatican II notes the Church’s special bond with Jews (CCC 839–840).
quiz: Abraham was told to…|Wait|Build a ship|Leave his country|Fight|2|Genesis 12:1.
God promised him…|Descendants and blessing|A throne|Gold|A tower|0|Genesis 12:2.
Abraham is called…|King of Egypt|Judge|Prophet of fire|Father of faith|3|Romans 4:11.
lessons.life: Take a faith step that scares you.
lessons.saint: Abraham: our father in faith, who left his homeland because God called him.
misc: “Abraham earned God’s favor by being good.”
“The promise to Abraham ended with the Old Testament.”
lessons.mem: “Abram believed the Lord, and he counted it to him as righteousness.” (Genesis 15:6)
lessons.hook: Ask: “Would you move to a place you’ve never seen because someone you trust asked you to?” Read Genesis 12:1–4.
lessons.assess: Ask students to name three parts of God’s promise to Abraham and how Abraham responded.

lessons.title: Isaac and Jacob
lessons.idea: God’s promise passes from Abraham to Isaac and to Jacob. Isaac’s near sacrifice shows Abraham’s faith and foreshadows Christ. Jacob wrestles with God and receives the name Israel.
lessons.question: What does Jacob’s new name mean?
lessons.activity: “Patriarchs compared” (30 min). Make a chart for Abraham, Isaac and Jacob: calling, test, mistake, promise, name. Include Genesis 22 (Isaac), 28 (Jacob’s ladder) and 32 (wrestling). Add where Jesus echoes them: John 1:51 (ladder).
teach: Isaac is the child of promise, born when Abraham and Sarah were old. In Genesis 22 God tests Abraham, then provides a ram; the church fathers saw Isaac carrying wood as a type of Christ carrying the cross (CCC 2572).
God does not desire human sacrifice; the story ends by showing that God provides the offering. Abraham’s faith that “God will provide” is fulfilled in Jesus.
Jacob’s ladder (Genesis 28) and wrestling at the Jabbok (Genesis 32) show a persistent seeker; he is renamed Israel, “one who strives with God” (CCC 2573).
God works with flawed people. Jacob was a deceiver, yet God kept his promise.
talk: What do we learn from Genesis 22?
How does God use flawed people?
quiz: God provided…|A goat|A ram|A bull|A lamb of silver|1|Genesis 22:13.
Jacob’s new name is…|Joseph|Isaac|Judah|Israel|3|Genesis 32:28.
Isaac foreshadows…|Elijah|Christ|Moses|David|1|CCC 2572.
lessons.life: Offer one thing to God this week.
lessons.saint: Jacob: who wrestled with God and received the name Israel.
lessons.mem: “God will provide for himself the lamb for a burnt offering, my son.” (Genesis 22:8)
lessons.hook: Read Genesis 22:1–2 and stop. Ask students to describe how Abraham felt. Then read the rest quickly and ask: “What did God show?”
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain how Genesis 22 points to Christ.

lessons.title: Joseph: from slavery to rescue
lessons.idea: Joseph, sold by his brothers, rose from slavery to rule Egypt and saved his family from famine. He forgave them and said, “You meant evil against me, but God meant it for good.” His story shows divine providence.
lessons.question: How does Joseph forgive?
lessons.activity: “Role-play Genesis 45” (30 min). Act the reunion scene: Joseph reveals himself, the brothers react, Joseph forgives. Discuss: How does forgiveness change the story? Compare with Jesus’ forgiveness from the Cross.
teach: Joseph’s story takes the family from Canaan to Egypt (Genesis 37–50). It sets the stage for the Exodus.

God’s providence: he guides all things to their end without removing human freedom (CCC 302–314). Evil is never willed by God but he can draw good from it (CCC 311–312). “You meant evil against me; but God meant it for good” (Genesis 50:20).
Joseph is a type of Christ: beloved son, betrayed by brothers, sold, raised from a pit to save the people (CCC 128–130).
Speak carefully on suffering: this verse does not justify abuse. God works through but does not cause the evil of others.
talk: Where do you see good from evil?
quiz: Joseph was sold by…|Potiphar|Moses|His brothers|Pharaoh|2|Genesis 37.
Joseph said God meant it for…|Loss|Good|Fame|Evil|1|Genesis 50:20.
Providence is…|God’s care for creation|Fate|Control|Luck|0|CCC 302.
lessons.life: Forgive someone who has hurt you.
lessons.saint: Joseph: the quiet carpenter who protected Mary and Jesus and trusted God’s word in dreams.
lessons.mem: “You meant evil against me, but God meant it for good.” (Genesis 50:20)
lessons.hook: Show a brightly colored coat. Ask, “What happens when a family has favorites?” Read the story of the coat in Genesis 37.
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain providence using Joseph and to name one way Joseph is like Jesus.

units.title: Exodus and the Law
units.eq: How does God save and teach?

lessons.title: The call of Moses
lessons.idea: God heard Israel’s cry in Egypt and called Moses at the burning bush. He revealed his name, “I AM WHO I AM” (YHWH), and promised to be with his people and set them free.
lessons.question: How does God reveal his name?
lessons.activity: “The name” study (25 min). Read Exodus 3:1–15. Students write what the bush, the sandals, the name and Moses’ excuses show. Note how the Jews revere the name (“Adonai”). Compare with Jesus’ “I am” sayings in John (e.g., 8:58; 6:35).
teach: God reveals his name YHWH, “I am who I am” (Exodus 3:14; CCC 203–213). It expresses that God is, he is faithful and he is with us.
The Jews avoid pronouncing the name; the Church follows by reading “Lord” (CCC 209). Jesus’ “I am” echoes the divine name (John 8:58; CCC 211).
God calls Moses despite his reluctance. The call shows that God sends the weak (Exodus 3:11). The holy ground teaches reverence (CCC 2144).
Present God as both transcendent (fire) and near (he hears).
talk: What does God say about suffering?
quiz: God’s name is revealed as…|Lord of war|The Great One|King|I AM|3|Exodus 3:14.
Moses was called at…|Mt Zion|Babel|The burning bush|The Red Sea|2|Exodus 3.
God hears…|Kings|Priests|Nobody|The cry of his people|3|Exodus 3:7.
lessons.life: Use God’s name only in prayer and respect.
lessons.saint: Moses: the shy shepherd God used to free Israel and give the Law.
lessons.mem: “I am who I am… Say this to the people of Israel: ‘I AM has sent me to you.’” (Exodus 3:14)
lessons.hook: Ask, “What do you do when you hear someone calling for help?” Read Exodus 3:7–8: “I have seen the affliction of my people.”
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain what God’s name tells us about him.

lessons.title: Passover and the Red Sea
lessons.idea: The Passover and the crossing of the Red Sea are Israel’s great salvation events. The lamb’s blood saved the firstborn, and God split the sea. Christians see the Passover fulfilled in Christ the Lamb and the Exodus in Baptism and the Eucharist.
lessons.question: How does Passover foreshadow Easter?
lessons.activity: “Passover to Eucharist” (30 min). Make a chart linking the elements: lamb → Lamb of God (John 1:29), blood on doorposts → blood of Christ, unleavened bread → Eucharistic bread, sea → Baptism (1 Corinthians 10:1–4). Then compare Exodus 12 to the Last Supper (Luke 22:7–20).
teach: Passover: the lamb, the blood, the unleavened bread, the haste (Exodus 12). It is celebrated each year as a memorial (CCC 1363). Israel remembers as if present.
The Red Sea is the climax: God saves by water and defeats Pharaoh (Exodus 14). The Fathers saw it as a type of Baptism (CCC 1221–1222).
Jesus is “the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world” (John 1:29). He died at Passover; the Last Supper was a Passover meal and the Mass is its new fulfillment (CCC 1340, 1363–1364).
The Easter Vigil reads Exodus 14. Point out the link.
talk: How is the Last Supper a Passover?
quiz: The blood of the lamb…|Saved the firstborn|Cleaned the house|Was thrown away|Fed Israel|0|Exodus 12:13.
Christ is the…|Judge|Shepherd of sheep|Lamb of God|King of kings only|2|John 1:29.
Israel crossed the…|Jordan|Dead Sea|Nile|Red Sea|3|Exodus 14.
lessons.life: Read Exodus 12 and John 1 and compare.
lessons.saint: John the Baptist: the forerunner who prepared the way and pointed to Christ.
misc: “Passover is only a Jewish festival with nothing to do with Christians.”
“The Last Supper was a normal dinner.”
lessons.mem: “Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world!” (John 1:29)
lessons.hook: Set out a plate with lamb (or a picture), unleavened bread, bitter herbs. Ask what each tells about being rescued in haste.
lessons.assess: Ask students to match three Passover elements with their fulfillment in Christ.

lessons.title: Sinai: the Law and covenant
lessons.idea: At Sinai, after saving Israel, God gave the Law as the way of covenant life. The Ten Commandments are a gift of freedom, summarizing love of God and love of neighbor.
lessons.question: How are the Ten Commandments a gift?
lessons.activity: “Commandments by theme” (25 min). Cards with the ten commandments; students sort into “love of God” (1–3) and “love of neighbor” (4–10) and rewrite each in one positive sentence. Then read Exodus 19:3–6 and 20:1–2 and note that God first rescues, then gives the law.
teach: God gave the Law after saving Israel (Exodus 20:2; CCC 2056–2063). It is a gift of freedom, not a price for salvation.
The Decalogue is divided in two tablets: love of God and love of neighbor (CCC 2067–2068). All people are bound by it because it expresses natural law (CCC 2070–2072).
Israel became “a kingdom of priests and a holy nation” (Exodus 19:6). The covenant is a relationship.
Our numbering follows Augustine; Jews and Protestants number differently. Mention it for curious students.
talk: Why did God give the Law?
quiz: The Ten Commandments were given at…|Jericho|Mount Carmel|Jordan|Mount Sinai|3|Exodus 19-20.
They begin with…|Love of self|Wealth|Love of God|Rules for kings|2|CCC 2083.
The Law is…|Obsolete|A trap|A gift|A burden only|2|CCC 2059.
lessons.life: Say the Ten Commandments aloud.
lessons.saint: Moses: the shy shepherd God used to free Israel and give the Law.
misc: “We keep the commandments to earn God’s love.”
lessons.mem: “I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery.” (Exodus 20:2)
lessons.hook: Ask: “Do rules make us free or boxed in? What about traffic rules?” Reflect that rules make life together possible and free.
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain why God gave the commandments after the Exodus, not before.

units.title: Kings and prophets
units.eq: How does God lead his people?

lessons.title: Samuel, Saul and David
lessons.idea: Israel asked for a king. After Saul failed, God chose David, a shepherd, “a man after his own heart.” God promised David an everlasting throne, a promise fulfilled in Jesus, Son of David.
lessons.question: What did God promise David?
lessons.activity: “David to Jesus family tree” (25 min). Draw a simple tree from David (1 Samuel 16) through Solomon to Joseph and Jesus (Matthew 1). Mark God’s promise in 2 Samuel 7:12–16 and the title “Son of David” (Matthew 1:1; Luke 1:32–33).
teach: Samuel anoints Saul and then David (1 Samuel 9–16). David is shepherd, warrior, king and psalmist (CCC 2579).
God’s covenant with David (2 Samuel 7) promises an eternal dynasty (CCC 709). The angel tells Mary her son will receive “the throne of his father David” (Luke 1:32).
David is a sinner too: Bathsheba and Uriah (2 Samuel 11–12). His repentance in Psalm 51 shows God’s mercy.
The Messiah (“anointed”) is the king from David’s line (CCC 436).
talk: How is Jesus the son of David?
quiz: David was anointed by…|Samuel|Elijah|Moses|Nathan|0|1 Samuel 16.
God promised David…|A city|A temple of gold|Peace only|An eternal throne|3|2 Samuel 7:16.
Messiah means…|Lord|King|Teacher|Anointed|3|CCC 436.
lessons.life: Pray a psalm of David.
lessons.saint: David: a shepherd and king who sinned, repented and wrote many of the Psalms.
misc: “Kings in the Bible ruled by their own right.”
lessons.mem: “The Lord looks on the heart.” (1 Samuel 16:7)
lessons.hook: Show a shepherd’s staff and a crown. Ask, “Who would you choose to be king?” Read 1 Samuel 16:7: “The Lord looks on the heart.”
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain how the promise to David points to Jesus.

lessons.title: Solomon and the Temple
lessons.idea: Solomon built the Temple in Jerusalem as God’s house, where sacrifices were offered and the people met God. It prefigures Christ’s body and the Church, and Solomon’s prayer is a model of intercession.
lessons.question: Why is the Temple important?
lessons.activity: “Temple model” (30 min). Build a model or diagram: courts of the Gentiles, of women, of Israel, of priests; the Holy Place; the Holy of Holies. Label the altar, lamp and ark. Read 1 Kings 8:22–30. Compare it to the church building.
teach: The Temple is the place of sacrifice and God’s presence (CCC 583–586). Solomon’s dedication prayer recognizes that heaven cannot contain God (1 Kings 8:27).
Jesus honored the Temple (John 2:16) and said, “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up,” speaking of his body (John 2:19–21).
The Church is the Temple of the Spirit (1 Corinthians 3:16; CCC 756, 797). Each baptized person is a living stone (1 Peter 2:5).
Solomon’s later idolatry led to the kingdom’s division (1 Kings 11); wisdom without fidelity is not enough.
quiz: The Temple was built by…|Solomon|Joshua|Moses|David|0|1 Kings 6.
Jesus called his body…|A boat|The Temple|A garden|A house|1|John 2:21.
The Church is also…|A club|A museum|An empire|God’s temple|3|1 Corinthians 3:16.
lessons.life: Visit a church and pray in silence.
lessons.saint: Solomon: the king who asked God for wisdom and built the Temple.
lessons.mem: “Do you not know that you are God’s temple and that God’s Spirit dwells in you?” (1 Corinthians 3:16)
lessons.hook: Show a photo of a cathedral. “Why do people build beautiful places for God?” Then read 1 Kings 8:27: “Will God dwell on the earth?”
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain how the Temple points to Christ and to the Church.

lessons.title: The prophets
lessons.idea: The prophets spoke God’s word to kings and people, calling them back to the covenant, defending the poor and announcing the Messiah. Isaiah’s call and the Suffering Servant show the heart of prophecy.
lessons.question: What is a prophet’s job?
lessons.activity: “Isaiah and the Gospel” (30 min). Read Isaiah 6:1–8 (call: “Here I am, send me”) and Isaiah 53 (the Servant). Students list how Isaiah 53 matches the Passion in the Gospels (Mark 15). Write a modern “prophetic” sentence about justice.
teach: A prophet speaks for God, calling to repentance, justice and hope; not mainly predicting the future (CCC 64, 702, 2581–2584). Elijah and Elisha, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel and the twelve minor prophets.
Isaiah’s call (Isaiah 6) shows God’s holiness; the Sanctus at Mass echoes “Holy, holy, holy.” Isaiah 53 describes the Servant who bears our sins (CCC 601).
Jesus is the fulfillment of prophecy (Luke 24:27; CCC 711–716). John the Baptist is the last and greatest prophet (CCC 719).
Prophets suffered for the truth; the Church has prophets in every age (CCC 904–907).
quiz: Prophets speak…|For kings|God’s word|The future only|For wealth|1|CCC 64.
Isaiah 53 describes…|A suffering servant|A tax collector|A king|A warrior|0|Isaiah 53.
The prophets point to…|Egypt|Rome|The Messiah|The temple|2|CCC 711.
lessons.life: Read Isaiah 53 and a Passion narrative.
lessons.saint: Isaiah: the prophet whose visions of the Messiah, especially the suffering servant, shaped the New Testament.
lessons.mem: “Here I am! Send me.” (Isaiah 6:8)
lessons.hook: Ask: “What happens when someone tells the truth to a powerful person?” Introduce the prophets as truth-tellers for God.
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain what a prophet does and give one example of Jesus fulfilling a prophecy.

lessons.title: The exile
lessons.idea: When Israel and Judah broke the covenant, Assyria and Babylon conquered them and many were taken into exile. God did not abandon them: the prophets promised a return and a new covenant.
lessons.question: What hope does Jeremiah give?
lessons.activity: “Letter from Babylon” (30 min). After reading Jeremiah 29:4–14, students write a letter from an exile describing their grief and hope. Include “build houses, plant gardens, seek the welfare of the city” and “I know the plans I have for you.”
teach: The northern kingdom fell to Assyria in 722 BC; Jerusalem fell to Babylon in 587 BC (2 Kings 25). The exile was a judgment and also a purification (CCC 710–711).

Jeremiah urged the exiles to settle and pray; Ezekiel promised a new heart and Spirit (Ezekiel 36:26; CCC 715). Jeremiah 31:31 promises a new covenant, which Jesus fulfills at the Last Supper (Luke 22:20).
A “remnant” returns, a theme that shapes the New Testament (CCC 711).
Link to refugees and displaced people today. Catholic social teaching calls us to welcome the stranger.
talk: Where do we feel like exiles?
quiz: Israel was taken to…|Greece|Rome|Babylon|Egypt|2|2 Kings 25.
Jeremiah told them to…|Return at once|Seek the welfare of the city|Rebel|Hide|1|Jeremiah 29:7.
The new covenant is promised in…|Psalm 23|Jeremiah 31|Job 1|Genesis 1|1|Jeremiah 31:31.
lessons.life: Pray for your city.
lessons.saint: Jeremiah: the prophet who wept over Israel and promised a new covenant.
lessons.mem: “For I know the plans I have for you, declares the Lord, plans for welfare and not for evil, to give you a future and a hope.” (Jeremiah 29:11)
lessons.hook: Ask: “What would you take if you had to leave home in an hour?” Imagine being far from home for 70 years.
lessons.assess: Ask students to name what Jeremiah tells the exiles and what promise God makes.

lessons.title: Restoration
lessons.idea: After seventy years God moved Cyrus of Persia to let the Jews return. They rebuilt the Temple and the walls, and under Ezra and Nehemiah renewed the covenant by reading the Law aloud.
lessons.question: How does the community renew?
lessons.activity: “Return timeline” (25 min). Students mark key dates: 539 Cyrus, 538 first return, 516 Temple, 458 Ezra, 445 Nehemiah. Read Nehemiah 8 and act the reading of the Law (stand, listen, weep, celebrate). Compare with the Liturgy of the Word.
teach: Cyrus’ decree (Ezra 1:1–4) shows God directs history, even through pagan kings (CCC 304–306).
The returnees rebuilt the Temple and walls despite opposition. Nehemiah rallies workers, who build with a tool in one hand and a weapon in the other (Nehemiah 4).
In Nehemiah 8 Ezra reads the Law; the people listen from dawn to noon, and the Levites explain. This is a model of proclaiming the Word and the homily (CCC 1154).
Many remained in the Diaspora. After this period Greek and Roman powers ruled. Judaism looked for the Messiah.
talk: How did the people respond to the Law?
quiz: Ezra read…|Psalms|A letter|The Law|Proverbs|2|Nehemiah 8.
Nehemiah rebuilt…|A ship|Babel|The wall|The ark|2|Nehemiah 2.
The people wept at…|The food|The music|The words of the Law|The trip|2|Nehemiah 8:9.
lessons.life: Read a Scripture passage aloud with your family.
lessons.saint: Nehemiah: the leader who rebuilt Jerusalem’s walls and renewed the covenant.
lessons.mem: “The joy of the Lord is your strength.” (Nehemiah 8:10)
lessons.hook: Show a half-built wall. Ask: “Who needs to work on it? Who needs to guard it?” Introduce Nehemiah.
lessons.assess: Ask students to retell the return and explain what Nehemiah 8 shows about God’s Word.

lessons.title: The Psalms and Wisdom
lessons.idea: The Psalms are Israel’s prayer book and the Church’s. They include praise, lament, thanksgiving and royal psalms. Wisdom books, like Proverbs, teach how to live: “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom.”
lessons.question: Which psalm resonates?
lessons.activity: “Write a psalm” (30 min). Review Psalm 1 (two ways) and Proverbs 1:7. Students choose a type (praise, lament, thanks) and write their own psalm with an opening, a honest complaint or joy, and a trust statement. Share volunteers’ psalms.
teach: The Psalms are the great prayer of the Church (CCC 2585–2589). Jesus prayed them (Luke 24:44; Psalm 22 on the Cross).
Types: praise (Ps 150), lament (Ps 22, 88), thanksgiving (Ps 138), royal (Ps 2, 110), wisdom (Ps 1), pilgrim (Ps 120–134). They teach us to bring all our feelings to God.
Wisdom literature: Proverbs, Job, Ecclesiastes, Song of Songs, Wisdom, Sirach. “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of knowledge” (Proverbs 1:7), meaning awe and reverence, not terror.
Job shows that suffering is not always punishment (CCC 309–310).
quiz: The Psalms number…|73|150|50|27|1|CCC 2585.
A lament is…|A cry of sorrow to God|A story|A feast|A law|0|Psalm 22.
Jesus quoted Psalm…|22 from the cross|23 only|1|150|0|Mark 15:34.
lessons.life: Pray a psalm each day.
lessons.saint: Ambrose: bishop of Milan, who taught Augustine and wrote on the sacraments.
lessons.mem: The Lord is my shepherd; I shall not want. (Psalm 23:1)
lessons.hook: Play a short chant of a psalm or read Psalm 23 aloud. Ask, “What feelings does it express?”
lessons.assess: Ask students to give an example of lament, praise and wisdom and explain why all belong in prayer.

units.title: Preparing for the Messiah
units.eq: How did the Old Testament point to Christ?

lessons.title: The promises of the Messiah
lessons.idea: The prophets promised a Messiah: born in Bethlehem, of a virgin, a king from David’s line, a suffering servant. The New Testament shows Jesus fulfilling these promises.
lessons.question: Which prophecies are fulfilled?
lessons.activity: “Prophecy and fulfillment chart” (30 min). Students match: Isaiah 7:14 / Matthew 1:22–23; Micah 5:2 / Matthew 2:5–6; Isaiah 9:1–2 / Matthew 4:14–16; Isaiah 53:5 / 1 Peter 2:24; Psalm 22:16–18 / John 19:23–24, 37; Zechariah 9:9 / Matthew 21:4–5. Discuss: Why does it matter that these were written long before?
teach: The prophets prepare for the Messiah (CCC 522–524, 711–716). Messiah (Hebrew) and Christ (Greek) mean “anointed.”
Different strands: a king (Psalm 2, Isaiah 9), a servant (Isaiah 53), a prophet like Moses (Deuteronomy 18:15), a priest (Psalm 110), a Son of Man (Daniel 7). Jesus unites them (CCC 436, 439–440).
Not every prophecy is a prediction. Matthew shows that history and Scripture find their meaning in Christ (CCC 128–130).
Be honest that some connections are deeper than literal. The Church reads the Old Testament in light of Christ.
quiz: Micah foretold the Messiah’s birth in…|Bethlehem|Cana|Jerusalem|Nazareth|0|Micah 5:1.
Isaiah 7:14 speaks of…|A tree|A queen|The virgin who will conceive|A flood|2|Matthew 1:23.
Fulfilment means…|A rule|Prophecy abandoned|A coincidence|Prophecy realized in Christ|3|CCC 128.
lessons.life: Create a chart of three prophecies.
lessons.saint: John the Baptist: the forerunner who prepared the way and pointed to Christ.
misc: “The prophets wrote with Jesus’ name in mind.”
“Jews were wrong not to see it.”
lessons.mem: “But you, O Bethlehem Ephrathah… from you shall come forth for me one who is to be ruler in Israel.” (Micah 5:2)
lessons.hook: Show a pair of puzzle pieces. “Prophecy and fulfillment fit.” Read Micah 5:2 and Matthew 2:1–6.
lessons.assess: Ask students to give three prophecies with their fulfillments.

lessons.title: Types of Christ
lessons.idea: A type is a person, event or thing in the Old Testament that foreshadows Christ. Adam, Isaac, Moses, the manna, the bronze serpent and Jonah all point to him. The New Testament is hidden in the Old; the Old is made clear in the New.
lessons.question: What is a type?
lessons.activity: “Match types” (25 min). Cards: Adam (Romans 5:14), Isaac (Genesis 22), Moses (Deuteronomy 18), manna (John 6:31–35), bronze serpent (John 3:14–15), Jonah (Matthew 12:40), Melchizedek (Hebrews 7), the Temple. Students match each with Jesus and say what they share.
teach: Typology: the Old Testament’s persons and events are real and also point forward (CCC 128–130). “The New is hidden in the Old and the Old is unveiled in the New” (St Augustine).
Hebrews 8–9 explains that the earthly priests and tabernacle were a shadow of the heavenly (Hebrews 8:5). Christ is the high priest and the sacrifice (CCC 1544).
Adam is “a type of the one who was to come” (Romans 5:14). Jesus is the new Adam; Mary is the new Eve (CCC 411).
Warn gently against reading everything as a type; use the Church’s tradition as a guide.
quiz: Manna foreshadows…|Confession|Baptism|Marriage|The Eucharist|3|John 6:31-35.
The bronze serpent foreshadows…|The Cross|A king|The ark|A flood|0|John 3:14.
Adam is a type of…|Moses|David|Satan|Christ|3|Romans 5:14.
lessons.life: Look for a type of Christ in tonight’s reading.
lessons.saint: Augustine: who searched for truth for years before writing, “Our heart is restless until it rests in you.”
misc: “Typology makes the Old Testament less real.”
lessons.mem: “These are a shadow of what is to come, but the substance belongs to Christ.” (Colossians 2:17)
lessons.hook: Show a shadow of an object and ask what it is. Then reveal the object. “The Old Testament cast shadows; Jesus is the reality.”
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain one type and its fulfillment.

lessons.title: The Old Testament in the liturgy
lessons.idea: At Mass the Old Testament is proclaimed and prayed: the first reading is chosen to harmonize with the Gospel, and the responsorial psalm answers it. Jesus read Isaiah in the synagogue and declared, “Today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing.”
lessons.question: Which readings do you remember?
lessons.activity: “This Sunday’s first reading” (25 min). Look up this Sunday’s readings. Students identify the first reading, psalm and Gospel, find the link, and write one sentence on how they connect. Then pray the psalm aloud together.
teach: The Old Testament is part of the Church’s liturgy (CCC 1093–1095). The Church reads it as the preparation for Christ and sees the Eucharist as the fulfillment (CCC 1094).
The Sunday cycle (A, B, C) and the Easter Vigil’s seven readings give a sweep of salvation history (CCC 1154). The first reading usually fits the Gospel theme.
The responsorial psalm is a meditation on the first reading. The Church’s hymns also use the psalms and canticles.
The Old Testament is not obsolete (CCC 121–123). Marcionism, which rejected it, was condemned.
talk: Why does the Church read the Old Testament?
quiz: The first reading is usually from…|Revelation|The Old Testament|A letter|The Gospel|1|CCC 1093.
The responsorial psalm responds to…|The first reading|The creed|The Gospel|The homily|0|GIRM.
The Church reads the Old Testament because…|It is short|It is easy|It is old|It prepares for Christ|3|CCC 121.
lessons.life: Compare this Sunday’s first reading and Gospel.
lessons.saint: Jerome: who translated the Bible into Latin and wrote, “Ignorance of Scripture is ignorance of Christ.”
misc: “We skip the Old Testament because it’s harsh.”
lessons.mem: “Today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing.” (Luke 4:21)
lessons.hook: Read Luke 4:16–21 and ask what Jesus did with the scroll. “He is the key to the Scriptures.”
lessons.assess: Ask students to identify the three readings in a given Sunday and explain how they connect.

units.title: Living the Old Testament faith today

lessons.title: The Ten Commandments for today
lessons.idea: The Ten Commandments still guide life today: in friendships, school, technology, family and money. They are a path of love, summed up by Jesus in two commands. Applying them takes thought and conscience.
lessons.question: How do they apply now?
lessons.activity: “Debate the scenario” (30 min). Teams get cases (online rumors, cheating, ignoring a lonely classmate, Sunday sports, gossip) and decide which commandments apply, what a loving response is, and what it costs. Present to class.
teach: The Commandments are a path of love with a positive core (CCC 2052–2074). Each prohibition protects a good and implies a duty.

Applications: first commandment, putting God first (also over gadgets); second, respecting God’s name; third, Sunday; fourth, family; fifth, respect for life including bullying; sixth and ninth, purity; seventh, honesty and fairness; eighth, truth online; tenth, contentment (CCC 2083–2557).
Grave sins can be committed in the heart as well as in deed (Matthew 5:21–30). Conscience must be formed (CCC 1783).
Ask students to apply them with courage, not fear.
talk: How does a commandment apply to social media?
quiz: Natural law is…|Church law only|A law of physics|The moral law known by reason|Civil law|2|CCC 1954.
The Commandments are…|Optional|Cultural|Temporary|Always binding|3|CCC 2072.
The Decalogue summarizes…|Temple rites|Love of God and neighbor|Taxes|Rules of war|1|CCC 2055.
lessons.life: Apply one commandment to your online behavior.
lessons.saint: Carlo Acutis: a teenager who loved the Eucharist, used computers to share the faith and died at 15.
misc: “If no one gets hurt it’s not a sin.”
lessons.mem: “If you love me, you will keep my commandments.” (John 14:15)
lessons.hook: Describe a school scenario: a friend asks you to share answers during a test, or posts a rude picture online. “Which commandment is in play?”
lessons.assess: Present a new scenario and ask students to apply two commandments and propose a loving response.

lessons.title: Justice and mercy
lessons.idea: The prophets demanded justice for the poor and mercy for the weak. “Let justice roll down like waters.” Catholic social teaching continues this call: human dignity, the common good, solidarity and care for the poor.
lessons.question: What does God require?
lessons.activity: “Justice project” (30 min). Students identify a need (hunger, loneliness, creation) and plan a project with Micah 6:8 as its motto: do justice, love kindness, walk humbly. Fill in who, what, when, and how prayer will support it.
teach: Amos, Isaiah and Micah condemned empty worship without justice (Amos 5:21–24; Isaiah 1:11–17). God hears the cry of the poor (CCC 2443–2446).
Catholic social teaching has principles: dignity of the person, the common good, subsidiarity, solidarity, preferential option for the poor (CCC 1905–1912, 2443–2449).
Justice gives each their due; mercy goes beyond it. Together they reflect God (CCC 1807, 2447).
Link to the works of mercy and to Pope Francis’ call to care for the poor.
quiz: Micah 6:8 says to do justice, love mercy and…|Walk humbly|Sing|Rest|Fight|0|Micah 6:8.
Amos wanted justice to…|Be taxed|Be hidden|Be silent|Roll down like waters|3|Amos 5:24.
The poor are…|Close to God’s heart|Lazy|Ignored|Dangerous|0|CCC 2448.
lessons.life: Do a justice project this month.
lessons.saint: Dorothy Day: a journalist who founded the Catholic Worker movement to serve the poor.
lessons.mem: “He has told you, O man, what is good; and what does the Lord require of you but to do justice, and to love kindness, and to walk humbly with your God?” (Micah 6:8)
lessons.hook: Show a photo of a food line or a homeless shelter. Read Amos 5:24 and ask, “What is God asking?”
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain Micah 6:8 and name one way to live it.

lessons.title: Prayer with the psalms
lessons.idea: Lectio divina is a way to pray with Scripture: read, meditate, pray, contemplate. Praying the Psalms with Jesus and with the Church unites our voices to the prayer of millions.
lessons.question: Which psalm do you use?
lessons.activity: “Lectio with a psalm” (25 min). Lead Lectio divina with Psalm 23: read slowly, notice a word; read again and meditate on it; pray in response; rest in silence; resolve a small action. Journal a line from the experience.
teach: Lectio divina has four moments: lectio (read), meditatio (reflect), oratio (pray), contemplatio (rest), and often actio (act) (CCC 2705–2708).
The Psalms give words to every human emotion and are Christ’s own prayer, which we pray in him (CCC 2587–2589). Psalm 51 teaches repentance; Psalm 23 trust.
The Church prays the Psalms in Mass and the Liturgy of the Hours (CCC 1174–1178).
Encourage a daily habit: one psalm a day, or the Sunday psalm all week.
quiz: Lectio divina begins with…|Speaking|Singing|Sleeping|Reading|3|CCC 2708.
Psalm 23 begins…|Blessed is the man|The Lord is my shepherd|Out of the depths|Have mercy|1|Psalm 23.
Psalm 51 is…|A harvest song|A wedding song|A battle song|A penitential psalm|3|Psalm 51.
lessons.life: Pray Psalm 23 or 51 nightly.
lessons.saint: Bernard: a Cistercian abbot whose sermons on Scripture and the love of God are still read.
misc: “I need to feel something to pray.”
lessons.mem: “Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within me.” (Psalm 51:10)
lessons.hook: Ask: “How can the same words mean something new each time you read them?” Show Psalm 23 and invite silence.
lessons.assess: Ask students to walk through the four steps of Lectio divina and share a word or phrase from the psalm.
